tier_reason: First-party nanobench tables in docs/module_json.md; the benchmark code (benchmarks/module_json/parse_serialize.cpp) is public, but the page gives no compiler, flags, or CPU model, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Faster than nlohmann::json at parsing: 2.2x on twitter.json (402.89 vs 182.76 op/s), 2.4x on apache_builds.json (2,134.76 vs 881.03 op/s), and about 4x on strings.json and numbers.json (derived from page data). Faster than nlohmann at serializing by about 1.6-1.9x on twitter.json and apache_builds.json (e.g. twitter.json minimized: 834.42 vs 440.27 op/s), 1.5x on numbers.json, and 2.4x on strings.json (derived from page data). Vs RapidJSON, utl::json wins only strings.json parsing and most serialization runs. The author says that an experimental flat-map object type (not the shipped default) 'allowed utl::json to beat RapidJSON on all serializing tasks and significantly closed the gap of database.json parsing'. RapidJSON is still 1.30-1.40x faster at parsing database.json in that run.
corrections.caveats: No CPU model, compiler, or compiler flags appear on the benchmark page (nanobench tables showing relative %, ms/op, op/s, and err% only), so the methodology is self-reported and partial. The 'relative' column is relative to utl::json, and >100% means faster. RapidJSON beats utl::json on parsing on every file except strings.json: numbers.json 1.29-1.45x, twitter.json 2.07-2.22x, apache_builds.json 1.63-1.72x, database.json 1.30-1.40x. It also roughly ties utl::json at serializing apache_builds.json (100.5%). The consistent win is only against nlohmann and PicoJSON. The database.json/flat-map result uses a configuration the author rejected, so it does not describe the shipped library. The page also warns that Clang/libc++ below version 20 falls back to a much slower number parser (no std::from_chars).

notes: The numbers are on the page and belong to the utl::json rows. The serialization range was overstated: the record claimed 1.9-2.4x on twitter/apache, but the page gives 1.6-1.9x. 'Closed most of the parsing gap' was also overstated; the page says 'significantly closed', and RapidJSON is still about 1.3-1.4x faster. The caveat undercounted RapidJSON's parsing wins.
